episode_title: Six More Stories That Should Be Films

stories.topic: Swimming Instead of IIT (A Goodhart's Law Fable)
stories.summary: Entrepreneur Deepak VS proposed a thought experiment: replace IIT entrance exams with a swimming test. India has plenty of coastline; the engineers we'd get would be just as good because the test selects for hunger, passion, initiative. Amit got carried away with enthusiasm; Deepak corrected him: by year two, Kota would have swimming coaches in Speedos on billboards and the system would be gamified all over again. From this seed, Amit constructs a fictional film about a young man who actually loves engineering but is forced into the swimming-pool treadmill, finds liberation in the open sea beyond the safety markers, and then walks into the storm.
stories.insight: Once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Any selection mechanism — no matter how clever or unconventional — will be gamed and hollowed out. The deeper allegory: the joy of learning lives outside the lane, in the open sea, but the system rewards only those who race between the markers.

stories.summary: Amit recites Smith's poem in full as a kind of ending to the swimming story: 'Nobody heard him, the dead man, but still he lay moaning. I was much further out than you thought, and not waving but drowning... Oh no, no, no, it was too cold always, still the dead one lay moaning. I was much too far out all my life, and not waving but drowning.'
stories.insight: A reminder that other people's struggles are often invisible to us — what looks like a wave from shore may be the gesture of someone drowning. The poem doubles as a metaphor for the IIT-aspirant story: striving in plain sight while no one notices the suffocation.

stories.topic: The Lost Plutonium of Nanda Devi
stories.summary: In the late 1950s the CIA wanted to monitor Chinese nuclear tests on the Tibetan Plateau. Spy satellites weren't yet good enough, so they proposed hauling a plutonium-powered listening device up Kanchenjunga. Indian mountaineers, just back from the climb, refused — the 70kg battery was impossible to take that high. They suggested Nanda Devi instead. A joint Indian-American team lashed the equipment to rocks during a sudden storm, planning to mount it days later. When they returned, the entire site was unrecognisable and the device was gone. To prevent a hiker from stumbling on it, the government invented a cover story about ecological protection and shut Nanda Devi to all access. The plutonium has never been found; one theory is that, because it stays warm by radioactive decay, it melted itself down hundreds of meters into the glacier.
stories.insight: Reality is not obliged to be reasonable. As an elevator pitch — 'CIA, India, China, plutonium, Himalayas, dead hippies, contaminated Ganga, half-life of thousands of years' — it would be rejected as word salad. Yet every word is true. A second insight: cover stories sometimes outlive the secret they were invented to hide; the 'pristine biosphere reserve' framing has become the public memory.

stories.topic: The NKVD Guard, the Plutonium, and the Frostbitten Ear
stories.summary: While the Soviets built their atom bomb, NKVD guards under Beria suspected the physicists of malingering. One guard burst in on a physicist holding plutonium, accused him of fobbing off stainless steel, and demanded proof. The physicist remembered plutonium's continuous radioactive decay keeps it warm. He told the guard to stand outside in -20 degrees holding it. The guard's ears got frostbite, his body froze, but the metal stayed warm in his hand. The guard returned: 'Okay, very well. Then I'll kill you tomorrow.'
stories.insight: A perfect distillation of how science survived under Stalinism — by demonstrating physical phenomena to people who had the power to kill but not the literacy to understand. Also the only context in which 'I'll kill you tomorrow' becomes weirdly tender.

stories.topic: The Delhi Renaissance and the Story of Delhi College (1803-1857)
stories.summary: In the half-century between the East India Company's defeat of the Marathas (1803) and the 1857 Mutiny, Delhi was a city in churn. The Mughals were nominal rulers; real power had shifted; Persian — the lingua franca of the elite — was being displaced by English over a single generation, leaving older Indians stranded in their own city. Delhi College, endowed by Fazl-i-Ali on the condition that teaching be done in local languages, became the unlikely meeting point: Western knowledge taught in Urdu, often without the technical vocabulary to support it. Out of this churn came astonishing figures — Ramchandra, a self-taught mathematician hailed by Augustus De Morgan as a kind of Indian peer to Ramanujan, who fearlessly attacked all religious orthodoxy and then — inexplicably — converted to Christianity at 30. Ghalib was simultaneously a literary legend and a man begging the British for a pension. The Delhi Urdu Akhbar carried news from Afghanistan to France and ran an editorial arguing for widow remarriage in 1841. Newspapers sold not on gossip but on poetry. Then 1857 swept it all away: the British framed the rebellion as a Muslim uprising, sowed the seeds of communal divide, and Delhi College dissolved into nothing — Ramchandra ended up headmaster of a random school.
stories.insight: A lost path of Indian modernity. We tend to imagine modernisation as a single, colonial track, but Delhi between 1803 and 1857 was already running an alternative — a synthesis where Urdu carried calculus and the public devoured editorials about widow remarriage. 1857 didn't just crush a rebellion; it ended a particular cosmopolitan-syncretic experiment that has no real successor.

stories.topic: Ramchandra: The Indian Mathematician Hardy Forgot
stories.summary: Ramchandra, born 1821, taught at Delhi College and tried to derive the rules of differential calculus using only algebra. He published a treatise that reached Augustus De Morgan in London, who was so impressed he tried to promote Ramchandra in the way Hardy would later promote Ramanujan. He failed. Ramchandra was also a fearless rationalist who attacked every religion — and then mysteriously converted to Christianity at thirty. After 1857, he ended his career as the headmaster of a small school.
stories.insight: A reminder of how thin the membrane is between a Ramanujan-style canonisation and obscurity — same continent, same century, same mathematical fire, opposite outcomes. Ramchandra's story is also a warning about how political ruptures (1857) can wipe out not just institutions but lineages of thought.

stories.topic: Sayyid Ahmad Khan Hires Six Tutors at Thirty
stories.summary: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, the founder of Aligarh Muslim University, was educated by private tutors until twenty, then went out into the world and made a name for himself. At thirty — middle-aged by 19th-century life expectancy — he decided he didn't know enough. So he hired six private tutors for six different subjects and sat through their lessons, an established public man going back to school.
stories.insight: Real intellectual life requires the humility to admit you don't know enough, even after the world has decided you're an authority. The mark of seriousness is that you keep building, even when the social cost is admitting publicly that you have gaps.

stories.topic: Newspapers Sold on Poetry, Not Gossip
stories.summary: In 1840s Delhi, the star attraction of any newspaper was poetry. Poets were the public figures of their time; their verses sold issues. Mushairas were so popular that one Karimuddin, who didn't even particularly care about poetry, started organising regular mushairas just so he could publish the tazkira (the printed record of what was recited) — a commercial calculation that ended up subsidising the poetry scene itself.
stories.insight: A vivid counter-data point against any 'human nature is fixed' theory of mass media. The same species that today buys tabloids about celebrities once paid to read meter and metaphor. What we consume is not predetermined by biology — it is shaped by which forms get distributed, which get celebrated, and what status accrues to whom.

stories.topic: The German Navy Scuttles Itself at Scapa Flow
stories.summary: After WWI, the Treaty of Versailles required Germany to deliver its entire freshly-minted Navy — 70+ warships, more than 100 submarines — to the Royal Navy at Scapa Flow at the top of Scotland. The German sailors were treated badly during the handover, with insufficient food and sanitation. On the appointed day, instead of handing over the fleet, they had pre-mounted explosives at the right places. One by one, on a clock, every minute or so, another ship blew up and went down. Many sailors died in the badly-evacuated explosions. The British inherited a fleet of wrecks at the bottom of the harbor.
stories.insight: A dramatic moral hard case. A soldier should follow orders — that is the deal. But what about an order to surrender your country's strategic strength to its rival? At Mers-el-Kebir, French sailors obeyed orders, refused to defect to the British, and were destroyed. At Scapa Flow, German sailors disobeyed and scuttled their fleet. History calls one tragedy and the other defiance — but the moral logic is identical, and it depends entirely on whose side you happened to end up on.

stories.topic: The Stories That Knit Together — Geiger Counters Made From Pre-Atomic Steel
stories.summary: Since the first atom bomb test in 1945, radioactive dust has contaminated the entire atmosphere — and therefore every iron mine, coal seam, and steel mill on Earth. Modern Geiger counters, which need to detect tiny radioactive signals, can't be built from contaminated steel; the discriminating power vanishes. The solution: divers go down to Scapa Flow and cut pieces from the scuttled German warships, made of beautiful pre-1945 'low-background steel.' That same steel ended up in the Geiger counters used to search Nanda Devi for the lost CIA plutonium.
stories.insight: A breathtaking demonstration of how stories tied together by chance illuminate the real connectedness of the world. A 1919 act of mutiny in Scotland produced the only material capable of detecting a 1965 American spy mission's lost plutonium in the Himalayas. As Ajay says: 'See stories and stories are all coming together. Mers-el-Kebir and Nanda Devi and now Scapa Flow. The tapestry of the world brings everything together.'

stories.summary: Amit pitches a low-budget film about a community of naturalistic vloggers — phones-on-tables, real-life-as-it-happens. Early in the film: a vloggers' meet-up that becomes a 'Mexican standoff' of cameras instead of guns. Each vlogger appears in every other vlogger's frame; you cut between them and pull back to find a hall of mirrors. Then a new androgynous vlogger appears whose authenticity feels different from the rest, and the everyday-Joe protagonist falls in love.
stories.insight: A device for investigating what authenticity even means in an age of manufactured selves. The protagonist's love forces him to confront whether his attraction is conditional on the genitals beneath the gender presentation — which the film refuses to answer, instead leaving him to realise that the androgynous vlogger is the only person being true to themselves and that everyone else, gently and without villainy, is fake.

stories.topic: Sheep Parachuted to Italian Soldiers in Ethiopia
stories.summary: In 1935, Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia stalled when 'unmartial' Italian soldiers — guys who just wanted a good time — found themselves marching through hot deserts and suffering through bad rations. Mama Mia, near-mutinies broke out. The Italian solution: in Italy, they strapped parachutes to live sheep, loaded them into planes, flew over the army camps, and pushed the sheep out one by one to drift gently down to the soldiers below. Why live sheep? In 1935, refrigeration was limited — the live sheep was its own life-support system, keeping the meat fresh until it landed. There exists at least one surviving (very blurry) black-and-white photograph.
stories.insight: A reminder that morale is logistics. A campaign of conquest can fail not because of brave defenders but because the invaders won't fight without good food. Also: the logistical creativity unlocked when the alternative is mutiny is genuinely impressive — there is something almost gentle about the image of a sheep drifting down on a parachute into a desert war.

recommendations.item: Inside the CIA Mission to Haul Plutonium Up the Himalayas
recommendations.creator: Robert Beckhusen
recommendations.context: Wired magazine's account of the CIA-led plutonium expedition to Nanda Devi, told from the American climbers' side.
recommendations.reason: The American end of the story Ajay tells. The article walks through how the CIA recruited America's elite mountaineers one by one, sworn to silence in exchange for an all-expenses-paid Himalayan climb.

recommendations.creator: Swapna Liddle
recommendations.context: Swapna Liddle's book on Delhi from 1803 to 1857 — the half-century of churn around Delhi College, Ghalib, the displacement of Persian, and the run-up to the Mutiny.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'the best book of quasi-Mughal history I have really come across.' The book is the source of his entire Delhi College story — the language transition, Ramchandra and De Morgan, the Delhi Urdu Akhbar's editorials, Karimuddin's tazkiras, and the cultural void that 1857 created.

core_ideas.concept: Goodhart's Law (and the Gamification of Selection)
core_ideas.explanation: Once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Whatever you select for, the system will be re-engineered to produce that measure cheaply — the underlying quality you actually wanted will be the first casualty. Replacing the IIT exam with a swimming test wouldn't liberate Indian engineering; by year two, Kota would have swimming coaches in Speedos on billboards. This isn't a flaw of one specific test — it's a feature of any single optimisable metric meeting a population of strivers and a coaching industry.
core_ideas.quote: What will happen in the second year is that the system will get gamified. Kota will start having swimming classes.

core_ideas.concept: Reality Is Not Obliged to Be Reasonable
core_ideas.explanation: Fiction has to make sense — characters need motivations, plots need plausibility, the elevator pitch has to land. Reality faces no such constraint. A story whose elevator pitch is 'CIA + India + China + plutonium + Himalayas + hippies + contaminated Ganga' would be laughed out of any pitch room, but every word of it is true. The implication for storytellers and intellectuals: the most fertile ground for narrative is often non-fiction, precisely because reality is allowed to be incoherent in ways imagination would never permit itself.
core_ideas.quote: The difference between reality and fiction is that reality is not obliged to be reasonable.

core_ideas.concept: Cover Stories That Outlive Their Secrets
core_ideas.explanation: When the Indian government couldn't tell the public it had lost a CIA plutonium device on Nanda Devi, it invented a cover story: the region is too ecologically precious, hippies are smoking dope and pitching tents, we have to shut it down for biodiversity. Decades later, the cover story has become the public memory; the original truth is a footnote in Wired magazine. Bureaucratic concealment doesn't just hide events — it actively rewrites the meaning of places, sometimes for generations.

core_ideas.concept: The Lingua Franca Crash (Persian to English in One Generation)
core_ideas.explanation: Delhi between 1803 and 1857 lived through something that almost never happens in history: a complete swap of the language of power. At the start, Persian was the language of all official documents, all elite communication, all letters of patronage — what English is to India today. Within fifty years, Persian was simply gone, leaving older Indians stranded — fluent in a dead currency. A ten-year-old could now look at his parents and see that their entire knowledge system had been devalued overnight. The trauma of this displacement is largely uncatalogued in popular history.
core_ideas.quote: If you are a kid who's ten years old, you look at your parents and they're completely helpless in the new world... it's like the ground beneath their feet has gone.

core_ideas.explanation: When Fazl-i-Ali endowed Delhi College on the condition that teaching happen in local languages, he forced an unusual experiment: Western mathematics, science, and history taught in Urdu — a language that lacked the technical vocabulary to carry them. The mismatch was generative. It produced figures like Ramchandra (who tried to derive calculus from algebra) and a public sphere (the Delhi Urdu Akhbar) where editorials on widow remarriage were printed in 1841. 1857 ended this path. The 'lost modernity' framing matters: India's modernisation didn't have to look like colonial imposition; for fifty years it briefly looked like cultural synthesis.

Even great reformers and rationalists are simultaneously immersed in personal currents that look unrecognisable from the outside — Ghalib begging for a pension while being a literary legend, Ram Mohan Roy writing obsequiously to the Mughal emperor while leading reform, Ramchandra mocking all religion and then converting to Christianity at thirty. The lesson: human beings are not 'rocks' with a single fixed character. They are rivers — different currents intersecting at the same point in time. Judging a public figure by one current ignores all the others.
core_ideas.quote: I think character is so contingent... My character is not a rock. My character is a river. It's flowing into different places, it's flowing into different shapes.

core_ideas.concept: The Moral Hard Case of Disobeying Orders
core_ideas.explanation: The Scapa Flow scuttling and the Mers-el-Kebir tragedy are the same moral structure with opposite outcomes. At Scapa Flow, German sailors disobeyed orders to surrender their fleet to the British and scuttled it. At Mers-el-Kebir, French sailors obeyed orders to remain neutral and were destroyed by the British. We applaud the German sailors and mourn the French — but the principle ('obey orders' vs 'follow conscience') is identical in both. The deeper observation: which side history canonises depends on the geopolitical outcome, not the moral logic of the act.
core_ideas.quote: If a soldier blows it up, it is right? If everyone starts rationalizing like that, you kinda get screwed.

core_ideas.explanation: Stories that look unrelated — a 1919 mutiny at Scapa Flow, a 1965 lost spy device at Nanda Devi — turn out to be physically connected: the only steel uncontaminated by post-1945 atmospheric radiation is the pre-atomic steel of warships sunk before nuclear testing began. So divers cut pieces from the German fleet at Scapa Flow, and that steel becomes the Geiger counters that search the Himalayas for lost American plutonium. The world is not a set of isolated narratives — it is a tapestry where the threads of disparate stories turn out to literally compose each other.
core_ideas.quote: The tapestry of the world brings everything together.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's working definition: authenticity is the laziest pose a person can take on — the one requiring the least effort to maintain. Anything else is exhausting; you can sustain a contrived self for a little while, but not for long, because we are each lazy beyond a point. By that logic, authenticity is not about depth or self-knowledge — it is just the equilibrium that the body settles into when no one is watching for long enough. Amit accepts the framing while adding a complication: the mask becomes the face. The pose you take on, even cynically, becomes you over time.
core_ideas.quote: Authenticity is the laziest pose you take on.

core_ideas.concept: Vloggers and the Question of Self-Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: The vlogger format — phone on the table, daily release — only works if the audience senses authenticity. But we may be authentic to ourselves and still not know ourselves: the public face and the private face are presented as identical, but neither may be true. Vlogging is therefore a peculiarly modern stress test of selfhood — a form whose minimum viable product is sincere self-presentation, performed by people who may not know what their sincere self even is.

core_ideas.concept: Love as the Realisation That Someone Else Is Real
core_ideas.explanation: Amit invokes Iris Murdoch: love is 'the extremely difficult realisation that someone other than oneself is real.' We all live with a kind of main character syndrome — a virtual reality in which we are the protagonist and everyone else is a prop. Love breaks the virtual reality: another consciousness must now be accounted for as real. The Murdochian reframe makes love less about feelings and more about an epistemic concession. Amit pairs it with his own provocation that lust is more honest than love because lust isn't pretending to be anything other than what it is.
core_ideas.quote: Love is the extremely difficult realization that someone other than oneself is real. — Iris Murdoch

core_ideas.explanation: Established science (and Amit's columns) suggest most of what we do, we don't do for the reasons we think we do. We act, then we construct a story explaining why. 'Love' may often be a cover for status-seeking, social acceptance, or companionship needs that have nothing to do with the romantic narrative we tell ourselves. This is not cynicism — it is an honest accounting of how brains actually generate behaviour, and how rationalisations get attached afterwards.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens by thanking the audience 'for wasting your life listening to us rambling.' Amit objects: 'They're not wasting their lives. We are going to tell them stories.'
Amit on the fictional IIT swimmer's training scene: imagining 'billboards on which they will have swimming coaches in Speedos.'

Ajay's NKVD guard punchline: after the physicist proves the metal is plutonium by having the guard hold it through frostbite, the guard responds — 'Okay, very well. Then I'll kill you tomorrow.' Ajay proposes it as their first piece of merch: a t-shirt that says 'Okay fine, I'll kill you tomorrow.'

Amit on pitching the Nanda Devi story as a movie: 'You'd say this is word salad — America, India, CIA, China, Plutonium, hippies, Nanda Devi.' Ajay's reply: 'Reality strung these words together and made a beautiful tapestry.'
Amit on the East India Company's curriculum at Delhi College: 'It's like we're teaching the Magna Carta, but we're doing it in Urdu.'
Ajay: 'These poor helpless Italian soldiers...' Amit interjects: 'I thought you were going to say kittens.'
Amit on the Scapa Flow steel: 'In a perverse way, the ships were more useful under the water than they would have been over the water.'
On ships sitting in harbours: Amit cites Otis Redding's '(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay' as the unofficial soundtrack of an inert German fleet.
On the German Navy's surrender at Scapa Flow: 'Think of an Amazon delivery happening. Now think of a delivery of a Navy.'

Ajay's deadpan on why live sheep instead of parachuted meat: 'The sheep is a life support system. It has an immune system, it keeps the meat fresh.' Amit adds: 'And also it can keep the soldiers company.'
Amit on the difficulty of pronunciation: he congratulates Ajay for successfully saying 'vlogging.' 'Many people can't do this. Achievement unlocked.'
Stevie Smith, 'Not Waving but Drowning' — quoted in full as the elegiac coda to the IIT-swimmer story.
Iris Murdoch: 'Love is the extremely difficult realization that someone other than oneself is real.' Used to frame the vlogger-falls-in-love story.
Reservoir Dogs / Tarantino — invoked for the 'Mexican standoff' homage, here reimagined with vloggers' cameras instead of guns.
'A ship is safe in the harbor, but that's not what ships are for.' Ajay borrows the proverb for the German Navy that sat out the entire First World War in dock.
Augustus De Morgan — the British mathematician who tried (and failed) to do for Ramchandra what G.H. Hardy would later do for Ramanujan.

The phrase 'malingerer' — Ajay notes it is one of those Russian/Soviet words that 'you got to be a communist to know,' used by the NKVD to justify executing physicists deemed insufficiently productive.

Mers-el-Kebir (1940) — the French naval base in Algeria where the British attacked French ships rather than let them fall to the Nazis, killing thousands. Ajay uses it as the moral mirror to Scapa Flow.
